{{Short description|German mathematician (1820–1906)}}
'''Gustav Conrad Bauer''' (18 November 1820, [[Augsburg]] – 3 April 1906, [[Munich]]) was a German mathematician,<ref name=NDBref>{{NDB|1|638|638|Bauer, Gustav|[[Georg Faber]]|116084642}}</ref> known for the Bauer-Muir transformation<ref>{{cite journal|last=Jacobsen|first= Lisa|authorlink= Lisa Lorentzen |title=On the Bauer-Muir transformation for continued fractions and its applications|journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications|volume=152|issue=2|year=1990|pages=496–514|doi=10.1016/0022-247X(90)90080-Y|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Bauer, G.|title=Von einem Kettenbruche Euler's und einem Theorem von Wallis|journal=Abhandlungen der Mathematisch-Physikalischen Classe der Königlich Bayerische Akademie der Wissenschaften|year=1872|volume=11|pages=96–116|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044106313281;view=1up;seq=425}}</ref> and Bauer's conic sections. He earned a footnote in the history of science as the doctoral advisor (''Doktorvater'') of [[Heinrich Burkhardt]], who became one of the two referees of [[Albert Einstein]]'s doctoral dissertation.

==Education and family==
Gustav Bauer passed in 1837 his ''[[Abitur]]'' at Augsburg's [[Gymnasium bei St. Anna]]. He continued his studies of mathematics at the Polytechnischen Schule Augsburg and also the universities of [[University of Erlangen|Erlangen]], [[University of Vienna|Vienna]] and [[Humboldt University of Berlin|Berlin]]. At Humboldt University in Berlin, Bauer received in 1842 his [[Promotion (Germany)|Promotierung]] under [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]]. From 1842 Gustav Bauer continued his studies in [[Paris]] under [[Joseph Liouville]], as well as other mathematicians.

In 1862 Gustav Bauer married Amalie, daughter of the ''Archivrat'' and Professor Honorarius Nathanael von Schlichtegroll. The marriage produced two daughters and a son Gustav junior, who became a well-known engineer.

==Professional career==
At the beginning of his professional employment, Bauer applied for a civil service position as a schoolteacher but became a private tutor from 1845 to 1853 in the royal house of Prince [[Mihail Sturdza]] and his successor Prince [[Grigore Alexandru Ghica]] in what is now Rumania. In 1857 Bauer spent three months in England and upon his return to Germany became a [[Privatdozent]] for the Mathematics Faculty of the [[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]]. There he received his [[Habilitation]] and became in 1865 professor extraordinarius, in 1869 professor ordinarius, and in 1900 professor emeritus.

Bauer's mathematical research dealt with algebra, geometric problems, [[spherical harmonics]], the [[gamma function]], and [[generalized continued fraction]]s. In 1871 Bauer was elected a full member of the [[Bayerische Akademie der Wissenschaften]]. In 1884 he was elected a member of the [[Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]]. His doctoral students include [[Heinrich Burkhardt]], [[Eduard Ritter von Weber]], and Christian August Vogler.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=61850}}</ref>

==Footnotes in the history of mathematics==
In [[Srinivasa Ramanujan|Ramanujan]]'s first letter to [[G. H. Hardy]], one of the theorems that impressed Hardy was:
: <math>1 - 5\left(\frac12\right)^3 + 9\left(\frac{1\times3}{2\times4}\right)^3 - 13\left(\frac{1\times3\times5}{2\times4\times6}\right)^3 + \cdots = \frac{2}{\pi}</math>

However, Bauer proved the theorem in 1859.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Bauer, G.|title=Von den Coefficienten der Reihen von Kugelfunctionen einer Variablen|journal=J. Reine Angew. Math.|year=1859|volume=1859|issue=56|pages=101–121|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015013784650;view=1up;seq=109|doi=10.1515/crll.1859.56.101|s2cid=122017325}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Berndt, Bruce C.|authorlink=Bruce C. Berndt|title=Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part 2|page=24|year=1999|publisher=Springer|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=z8Kjb0_pgx8C&pg=PA24|isbn=9780387967943}}</ref> Using a result of Bauer on generalized continued fractions, [[Oskar Perron]] published in 1952 the first proof of another formula of Ramanujan.<ref name=NDBref/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Perron, O.|title=Über eine Formel von Ramanujan|year=1952|journal=Sitz. Bayer. Akad. Wiss. München Math. Phys. Kl.|pages=197–213}}</ref>
